title: Nonnegative Variance Estimation and Ordered/Unordered Estimators
breadcrumb: Sampling theory → PPSWOR → Variance estimation and ordered estimators
engineName: Check pairwise variance coefficients and distinguish ordered from unordered estimators.
objectives: Explain why an unbiased variance estimate may be negative.
State the SYG variance estimator and its nonnegativity condition.
Explain limitations caused by zero joint inclusion probabilities.
Calculate Des Raj's ordered estimator and its variance for n=2.
Calculate Murthy's unordered estimator and explain its efficiency rationale.

prereq.name: First- and second-order inclusion probabilities
prereq.why: Variance estimators depend on π_i and π_ij.

prereq.name: Horvitz–Thompson estimator

traps: An unbiased variance estimator can be negative in a realised sample.
SYG nonnegativity requires the pairwise coefficient condition; it is not automatic for every design.
The usual pairwise variance estimator requires positive π_ij for relevant pairs.
Des Raj is order-dependent; Murthy is order-independent for n=2.
Use initial selection probabilities p_i in the Des Raj and Murthy formulas as defined for the observed units.
howto: For SYG, compute Δ_ij=π_iπ_j−π_ij and check its sign for every pair with positive π_ij. For Des Raj with two draws, retain draw order and apply the compact formula. For Murthy, use the unordered pair and the symmetric formula. Do not claim that all unbiased variance estimators are nonnegative.

scenes.title: Why variance estimates can be negative
scenes.objective: Distinguish true variance from an estimated variance.
body: A true variance is nonnegative by definition. A variance estimator is a random statistic calculated from the realised sample; an unbiased estimator can nevertheless take a negative value in some samples.
For the Horvitz–Thompson total estimator, the usual unbiased variance estimator uses first- and second-order inclusion probabilities. Its algebraic terms need not all be nonnegative.

The Sen–Yates–Grundy (SYG) form rewrites the variance estimator as a weighted sum of squared differences. Its nonnegativity depends on the sign of the pairwise coefficients and on positive joint inclusion probabilities.

items.ask: Can an unbiased variance estimator be negative?
items.recall: Yes. Unbiasedness is an expectation property, not a pointwise constraint.
refresh: An unbiased estimator is judged by its expectation over repeated samples from the design. A particular realised value can be below zero even when the parameter being estimated is nonnegative. This is possible for an unbiased variance estimator and does not mean the true variance is negative.

items.ask: Is the true variance ever negative?
items.recall: No. A variance is an expected squared deviation.
refresh: A variance is an expectation of a squared deviation, so the true design variance cannot be negative. Keep the parameter and its estimator separate: the parameter is nonnegative, while an unbiased estimator can have a negative realised value because it is a random variable.

items.ask: What does the SYG form use?
items.recall: Weighted squared differences of inverse-inclusion-probability values.
refresh: The Sen–Yates–Grundy form rewrites the variance using pairwise inclusion probabilities and squared differences between inverse-probability weighted values. It uses unordered pairs i<j. Its nonnegativity requires the relevant π_ij to be positive and π_iπ_j−π_ij to be nonnegative for every pair.

ask.q: What is the difference between unbiasedness and nonnegativity?
ask.nudge: Unbiasedness concerns the estimator's expectation; nonnegativity concerns every realised value.

scenes.title: A weighted squared-difference view
scenes.objective: Interpret the SYG estimator and its sign condition.
body: For a fixed-size design, define Δ_ij=π_iπ_j−π_ij. The SYG variance estimator for the total is one half the sum over sampled unordered pairs of (Δ_ij/π_ij)(y_i/π_i−y_j/π_j)².
Every squared difference is nonnegative. If π_ij is positive and Δ_ij is nonnegative for every pair, every term is nonnegative and the estimator cannot be negative.

If some Δ_ij is negative, a negative contribution is possible. This condition is sufficient for nonnegativity term by term; it is not a universal statement that every design has nonnegative SYG estimates.

scenario.teaser: Two units with unequal inclusion chances
scenario.title: The sign comes from the pair coefficient
body: Suppose a fixed-size sampling design has positive pairwise inclusion probability π_ij for every relevant pair. The SYG estimate uses the coefficient (π_iπ_j−π_ij)/π_ij multiplying a squared difference between y_i/π_i and y_j/π_j. If π_ij is no larger than π_iπ_j for every pair, all coefficients are nonnegative and the estimate is nonnegative for every sample. If the design violates this inequality for some pair, that pair contributes a negative term; the total estimate may or may not be negative depending on the observed values and the other pair contributions. Therefore the design condition is important, and it should not be replaced by the blanket claim that SYG is always nonnegative.
The design's joint inclusion probabilities, not merely its first-order probabilities, control this property.
scenario.q: What inequality gives nonnegative pair coefficients?

ask.q: Does one negative pair coefficient guarantee the entire estimate is negative?
ask.nudge: No. Other pair contributions may offset it.

scenes.title: Check a pair coefficient

viz.caption: The coefficient (π_iπ_j−π_ij)/π_ij is nonnegative when π_ij≤π_iπ_j.

body: Suppose π_i=0.4, π_j=0.5 and π_ij=0.15. Then π_iπ_j=0.20 and the SYG coefficient is (0.20−0.15)/0.15=1/3.
The coefficient is positive, and the squared difference cannot be negative. This pair's contribution is therefore nonnegative.
If π_ij=0.25 instead, the coefficient becomes (0.20−0.25)/0.25=−0.20. A negative pair contribution is possible.

ask.q: For π_i=0.4, π_j=0.5 and π_ij=0.25, what is the coefficient?

blocks.body: Ŷ_HT=Σ_{i∈s} y_i/π_i, where π_i>0 is the first-order inclusion probability.
v_HT(Ŷ)=Σ_{i∈s}Σ_{j∈s}[(π_ij−π_iπ_j)/π_ij](y_i/π_i)(y_j/π_j), when the required π_ij are positive. This unbiased estimator can be negative.
For a fixed-size design, v_SYG(Ŷ)=Σ_{i<j, i,j∈s}[(π_iπ_j−π_ij)/π_ij](y_i/π_i−y_j/π_j)². This is an unbiased alternative under the stated pairwise-probability conditions.

If π_ij>0 and π_ij≤π_iπ_j for every distinct pair, each SYG coefficient is nonnegative, so v_SYG≥0 for every realised sample. If the condition fails, the estimator may be negative; it is not universally nonnegative.

If π_ij=0 for a pair, the standard pairwise variance estimator cannot use that pair's observed joint-inclusion term. An unbiased design-based variance estimate may be unavailable without a different design or additional assumptions.

flow.title: Check a variance estimator
flow.alt: Confirm fixed sample size, check positive pair inclusion probabilities, compute pair coefficients, then assess whether every coefficient is nonnegative.
flow.note: If any pair probability is zero or a coefficient is negative, the usual guarantee does not apply.

ask.q: Does the HT variance estimator share the same simple nonnegativity guarantee?
ask.nudge: No. Its unbiased estimate can be negative.

scenes.title: Ordered estimators: Des Raj
scenes.objective: Construct the ordered estimator under sequential PPSWOR.

blocks.body: Under sequential PPS without replacement, selection probabilities change after each draw. The order of selection contains information used to construct an unbiased estimator.
Ŷ_d=(1/n)Σ_{r=1}^n t_r, where t_1=y_1/p_1 and t_r=Σ_{q<r}y_q + [y_r/p_r](1−Σ_{q<r}p_q), r≥2. Here p_r are the initial selection probabilities of the units in draw order.
v(Ŷ_d)=1/[n(n−1)] Σ_r (t_r−Ŷ_d)² = [Σ_r t_r²−nŶ_d²]/[n(n−1)]. This sample-variance form is nonnegative.

The estimator uses the ordered sequence. Reversing the order can change the estimate. Do not replace p_2 by a fixed unconditional draw probability: it is the initial probability of the second selected unit, while the conditional probability at draw two is adjusted after the first selection.

ask.q: Why can reversing two selected units change the Des Raj estimate?
ask.nudge: The first-draw probability enters the adjustment for the second draw.

scenario.teaser: PPS without replacement sample of two villages
scenario.title: Order changes the estimate
body: A survey selects two villages sequentially with probability proportional to a size measure and without replacement. The first selected village has initial probability p₁=0.2 and study value y₁=10; the second has initial probability p₂=0.3 and value y₂=12. Des Raj's estimator uses the first draw's probability in the correction for the second draw. The estimate is 46. If the draw order is reversed, the correction uses p₂ in the corresponding position and the result changes. The order is therefore part of the observed data required by this estimator.
The variance estimate is a nonnegative squared-difference expression for this two-draw case.
scenario.q: What feature of the observed sample must be retained?
scenario.answer: The order in which the two units were selected.

solution.why: These enter the estimator and variance.
The first draw receives its order-specific adjustment.
The squared difference makes this estimate nonnegative.

ask.q: Would reversing the two draws necessarily leave the estimate unchanged?

items.why: It is an expectation of a squared deviation.

items.claim: Every unbiased variance estimator must be nonnegative in every sample.
items.why: Unbiasedness concerns expectation, not each realised value.

items.claim: The SYG estimate is nonnegative if every relevant π_ij is positive and π_ij≤π_iπ_j.
items.why: Every pair coefficient and squared difference is then nonnegative.

items.claim: The HT variance estimator is always nonnegative.
items.why: The unbiased HT variance estimator can be negative.

items.claim: Des Raj's ordered estimator uses the order of selection.
items.why: The previous draws affect each adjusted term.

items.claim: Murthy's unordered estimator for n=2 depends on which unit was drawn first.
items.why: It symmetrises over both possible orders and depends on the unordered pair.

scenes.objective: Calculate the n=2 unordered estimate and variance.
scenes.problem: For two units with y₁=10, p₁=0.2 and y₂=12, p₂=0.4, calculate Murthy's unordered estimator and its variance estimate.
hints: Weight y₁/p₁ by 1−p₂ and y₂/p₂ by 1−p₁.
Use the corresponding nonnegative variance formula.
scenes.check: The estimator is invariant to order. The variance coefficient contains 1−p₁−p₂; here that factor is 0.4, not p₁+p₂=0.6.

solution.why: These are the two weighted values used in Murthy's formula.
The numerator weights each inverse-probability contribution by the other unit's non-selection probability.
The final factor is one minus the sum of the two initial draw probabilities.

ask.q: What is the main advantage of unordered estimation?
ask.nudge: It does not depend on the recorded draw order and can be more efficient by averaging over orders.

scenes.title: Variance and ordered/unordered checklist
scenes.objective: Summarise SYG, Des Raj and Murthy.
body: True variance is nonnegative, but unbiased variance estimators may be negative.
For fixed-size designs, the SYG form is a weighted sum of squared differences. It is guaranteed nonnegative when π_ij>0 and π_ij≤π_iπ_j for every distinct pair.
The HT variance estimator can be negative. Zero joint inclusion probabilities prevent the usual pairwise unbiased variance formula from using that pair.
Des Raj's ordered PPSWOR estimator uses draw order and has a nonnegative sample-variance estimate. For n=2, use the compact formulas in the lesson.

Murthy's unordered n=2 estimator averages the two ordered Des Raj estimates using their ordered-sample probabilities. It is symmetric in the two sampled units and is obtained by Rao–Blackwellisation/conditioning on the unordered sample; it is at least as efficient as the corresponding ordered estimator under the stated setup.

ask.q: Which estimator and key design condition should you remember for Nonnegative Variance Estimation and Ordered/Unordered Estimators?
ask.nudge: State the estimator, its weighting or expansion rule, and the assumptions behind its variance.

scenes.title: Mastery check
scenes.objective: Demonstrate independent command of nonnegative variance and ordered/unordered estimators.

sheet: SYG total variance estimate = Σ_{i<j in s}[(π_iπ_j−π_ij)/π_ij](y_i/π_i−y_j/π_j)².
SYG nonnegative if π_ij>0 and Δ_ij≥0 for all pairs.
HT variance estimate can be negative.
Des Raj: Ŷ_d=(1/n)Σt_r; t_r uses previous draws and initial p_r.
The SYG sum is over unordered sample pairs i<j, so each pair is counted once.
If any required π_ij=0, the usual pairwise HT/SYG variance expression is unavailable for that pair.
cards: In SYG, sum once over i<j; do not double-count (i,j) and (j,i).
tricks: Calculate Δ_ij before expanding the SYG sum.
For Des Raj, do not reorder observations.
For Murthy, swap unit labels and verify the estimate is unchanged.
shortcuts: A sum of nonnegative pair terms is nonnegative.
Murthy averages ordered estimates using their sample-order probabilities.
Check Δ_ij=π_iπ_j−π_ij pair by pair before claiming the SYG estimate is nonnegative.
remember: Unbiasedness is not the same as pointwise nonnegativity.
Rao–Blackwellisation explains the unordered estimator's efficiency advantage.

provenance: Author-created lesson for UGC NET Statistics Paper 2, Unit III-A, topic sampling-t9. Practice items are original and are not represented as official PYQs. Formulas are checked against Singh and Mangat, Elements of Survey Sampling, sections 4.7–4.8, and IIT Kanpur Sampling Theory Chapter 7. The SYG nonnegativity statement is conditional on positive pairwise inclusion probabilities and π_ij≤π_iπ_j for all relevant pairs; no blanket claim is made for arbitrary designs. Independent audit on 2026-11-14 corrected Murthy's n=2 unbiased variance estimator: the numerator factor is (1−p₁−p₂), not (p₁+p₂). The transfer example now uses p₁=0.2 and p₂=0.4 so the two expressions no longer coincide; exact arithmetic is checked in verify_sampling_t9.py.
